questions.q: In a loop, what is one iteration?
questions.explain: A loop runs its block again and again. Each single run of the block is one iteration.
options: The whole loop, from start to finish
One run of the loop's block

questions.q: You must print one line for every task in a list, and you do not know how long the list will be. What should you use?
questions.explain: A loop runs the same code as many times as needed, even when you do not know the number in advance. Writing lines by hand only works for a fixed, small number.
options: One console.log line per task, written by hand
A loop, which repeats the same block for each task
A switch with one case per task

questions.q: In for (let i = 1; i <= 5; i++), when does i <= 5 run?
questions.explain: let i = 1 runs once at the start, the condition i <= 5 is checked before every iteration, and i++ runs after every iteration.
options: Before every iteration; when it is false, the loop stops
After every iteration, to move the counter on
Only after the loop has finished

questions.q: In a for loop, what does the third part (for example i++) do?
questions.explain: The third part runs after each iteration. It does not have to be i++: n -= 2 or i-- work too.
options: It runs after every iteration and moves the counter on
It runs once before the loop starts
It decides whether the loop should stop
It runs only when the loop uses break

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The counter starts at 0 and the loop stops when i < 4 is false, so it runs for 0, 1, 2 and 3. line is a string, so += joins the digits instead of adding them.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The counter goes 10, 8, 6, 4, 2 and then stops, because 0 is not greater than 0. 10 + 8 + 6 + 4 + 2 is 30.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: 1 to 10 inclusive is 10 values, and 0 to 9 is also 10 values. Watch < versus <=: they decide whether the last value runs.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: After the last iteration, i++ makes i 3, then the check 3 < 3 is false and the loop ends. So i is 3 after the loop.

questions.q: When is a while loop the best choice?
questions.explain: Use while when you only know when to stop, like "until the balance reaches 200". For each item of a list, for...of is simpler.
options: When you want each item of a list
When you repeat until something happens and cannot know in advance how many times
When the body must always run at least once
When you want the keys of an object

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The value goes 2, 4, 8, 16, 32. After 16 the check 16 < 20 is still true, so one more step makes it 32. Then 32 < 20 is false and the loop stops.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: while checks the condition before the body, and 5 < 3 is false, so its body never runs. do...while checks after the body, so it always runs at least once.

questions.q: Which task fits a do...while loop best?
questions.explain: do...while always runs its body once, then checks. That matches "do this, then ask whether to do it again", like asking for input until it is valid.
options: Printing every item of a list
Asking the user for input, then asking again while it is not valid
Looping over the keys of an object

questions.q: This loop never ends: let balance = 100; while (balance < 200) { console.log(balance); }. Why?
questions.explain: A loop stops when its condition becomes false. If nothing in the body moves balance towards 200, that never happens. Always check that something inside the loop moves it towards the end.
options: A while loop needs a break to stop
Nothing inside the loop changes balance, so the condition stays true forever
console.log cannot be used inside a loop

questions.q: Your program hangs in the terminal because of an infinite loop. How do you stop it?
questions.explain: Ctrl+C stops the running program. Node does not stop a loop by itself; it runs forever.
options: Wait: Node stops any loop after one minute

questions.explain: for...of gives you each item of the list in turn, with no counter to manage.

questions.explain: for...of also works on strings, one character at a time. Each letter gets upper-cased and a dot is added after it.

questions.q: Why can you write for (const title of titles) with const, even though title gets a different value each time?
questions.explain: With for...of, every iteration creates a new title. Nothing reassigns it, so const is fine and is the usual choice.
options: Because const can be reassigned inside loops
Because each iteration gets a fresh title variable
Because the loop copies the whole array into title
It is a mistake; you must use let

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: for...in gives the keys (property names). task[key] reads the property whose name is stored in key.

questions.q: Someone used for...in on an array. What does this print?
questions.explain: On an array, for...in gives the positions, and as strings, not the items. Use for...of for arrays.
options:
Buy milk string
Call Ada string

questions.q: Which loop should you use to go over the items of an array?
questions.explain: for...of gives the items. for...in is for the keys of an object; on arrays it gives the positions as strings.

questions.q: What is the difference between break and continue in a loop?
questions.explain: break ends the loop immediately. continue works like a guard clause for one iteration: it jumps to the next one.
options: break skips one iteration; continue stops the loop
break stops the whole loop; continue skips the rest of this iteration and goes on with the next
break only works in switch; continue only in loops

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The empty string is skipped with continue. At "STOP", break ends the loop, so "c" is never reached.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: For even numbers, continue skips the rest of the iteration, so only the odd numbers are added. The loop itself keeps going until 6.

questions.q: How many times does the inner line run?
questions.explain: For every iteration of the outer loop, the inner loop runs completely. 3 rows × 4 columns = 12.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A break inside the inner loop only stops the inner loop. The outer loop goes on to row 2, where the inner loop starts again.

questions.q: You nest two loops, each over a list of 1000 items. About how many times does the inner body run?
questions.explain: Nested loops multiply: 1000 × 1000 is a million iterations. Keep that in mind before nesting loops over big lists.

questions.q: What does this print?

questions.q: You need both each item of a list and its position. Which loop does the lesson use?
questions.explain: A counting for loop gives you i, and list[i] reads the item at that position. for...of gives only the items.
options: A counting for loop with i from 0 to length - 1

questions.q: Which loop will you use most often for lists and strings?
questions.explain: for...of gives each item with no counter to manage. Use for when you need a counter or position, and for...in only for object keys.

questions.q: The checks are in the wrong order. What does this print?
questions.explain: 15 is a multiple of 3, so the first branch matches and the others are skipped. The check for 15 must come first.

questions.q: Why does the guessing game put the rules in checkGuess and play, separate from the keyboard code?
questions.explain: Code that reads the keyboard is hard to test. Put the logic in a function you can test with fixed input, and keep the keyboard part thin.
options: Because Node cannot run functions that read the keyboard
So the rules can be tested with a fixed list of guesses, since a test cannot type
Because readline only works inside a for loop
To make the program run faster

questions.q: A bad guess should not cost a try. What does this print?
questions.explain: "abc" is not a whole number and "" is empty, so continue skips them before tries++. Only "50" and "25" count.

questions.q: In the real game the secret number comes from Math.random(). Why is it a parameter of play(secret, guesses)?
questions.explain: A random secret would make the output different on every run. Passing it in lets the test fix it, so the output can be checked.
options: Because Math.random() does not work inside functions
So a test can choose the secret and get the same result every time
So the player can see the secret
Because parameters make the loop faster

questions.q: The interactive game uses node:readline/promises to read what the player types. Where does it run?
questions.explain: node: modules are built into Node.js, not the browser. The lesson runs the tested rules in the browser, and the keyboard game on your computer.
options: In the browser terminal on the lesson page
Only in Node.js on your computer
Anywhere, because readline is part of plain JavaScript

questions.q: Why are 7 tries always enough for a number from 1 to 100, if you always guess the middle?
questions.explain: Guessing the middle halves the numbers that are left. With 7 guesses you can always find the secret among up to 127 numbers (27 − 1), which covers 100. This is binary search.
options: Each guess halves the range, and 7 halvings can find the secret among up to 127 numbers (2 to the power of 7, minus 1)
Because the secret is never above 70
Because "too low" and "too high" each remove 10 numbers

questions.q: Use a for loop that counts down from 5 to 1 and builds one line, then print it after the loop. The program should print 5 4 3 2 1 go.
questions.explain: Start the counter at 5, keep going while i >= 1, and move it with i--.

questions.q: Finish sumTo(n) so it adds up every whole number from 1 to n with a loop. The program should print 15 5050 0.
questions.explain: Keep a running total and add the counter each iteration. For n = 0 the condition is false from the start, so the loop never runs and the total stays 0.

questions.q: Print the numbers 1 to 15 on one line, separated by spaces, but use Fizz for multiples of 3, Buzz for multiples of 5 and FizzBuzz for multiples of both.
questions.explain: Check for 15 first; otherwise 15 would match "multiple of 3" and stop there.
questions.expected: 1 2 Fizz 4 Buzz Fizz 7 8 Fizz Buzz 11 Fizz 13 14 FizzBuzz

questions.q: Finish countVowels(text) with a for...of loop over the string. Count the letters a, e, i, o and u, in lower or upper case. The program should print 2 5.
questions.explain: for...of gives one character at a time. Lower-case the text first, then check each letter with "aeiou".includes(letter).

questions.q: Find the first title longer than 10 characters, print Found at position N: TITLE, and stop looking. Use a counting for loop and break. The program should print Found at position 2: Write the quarterly report once.
questions.explain: You need the position, so a counting for loop fits. Without break, the last title would be printed too.
